quizName: DMV Practice Test #6 25 Questions • Passing Score 20

questions.question: What does a plastic, shatter-resistant face shield do?

options.text: It is not needed if you have a windshield.
It only protects your eyes.
It protects your whole face.
It does not protect as well as goggles.

questions.explanation: A face shield protects your whole face in a crash. Goggles only protect your eyes. A windshield is not enough protection by itself.

questions.question: When do most motorcycle crashes happen?

options.text: On short trips.
On long trips.
After riding for at least one hour.
After riding for more than 8 hours.

questions.explanation: Most motorcycle crashes happen on trips shorter than five miles, just a few minutes after the rider starts riding.

questions.question: If you carry a load in a sidecar, what happens to the motorcycle's stopping distance?

options.text: It may get longer.
It may get shorter.
It is not a concern.
It stays the same as a two-wheeled motorcycle.

questions.explanation: Adding weight to a motorcycle increases how long it takes to stop. Start slowing down and stopping earlier when carrying a load or passenger in a sidecar.

questions.question: Which of these should you NOT do to stay safe when riding at night?

options.text: Ride faster.
Ride slower.
Use your high beam headlight when possible.
Stay farther behind other vehicles.

questions.explanation: To ride safely at night, slow down, use your high beam headlight when no other vehicles are near, and increase your following distance. Watch for clues from vehicles ahead—their lights help light the road.

questions.question: When should you use extra space between you and other vehicles?

options.text: When roads are slippery.
When it is sunny outside.
When it is colder than usual.
When you are following other motorcycles.

questions.explanation: A two-second following distance is usually right. Use more space when conditions make it harder to stop, such as on wet or icy roads.

questions.question: Which is NOT a safe way to prevent fatigue while riding?

options.text: Protecting yourself from wind, cold, and rain.
Taking artificial stimulants.
Limiting how far you ride in one day.
Taking frequent breaks.

questions.explanation: On long trips, take frequent breaks and do not ride more than six hours in one day. Dress to protect yourself from the elements. Do not use artificial stimulants—the effects can be dangerous when they wear off.

questions.question: Where do most crashes happen?

options.text: Far from home.
On short trips.
On long rides.
Several hours into the ride.

questions.explanation: Most crashes happen on trips shorter than five miles, just a few minutes after the rider starts riding.

questions.question: Which of these provides the best protection for your face?

options.text: Sunglasses.
Windshield.
Goggles.
Face shield.

questions.explanation: A face shield protects your entire face in a crash. Goggles only protect your eyes. A windshield is not enough protection.

questions.question: How much of a motorcycle's total braking power comes from the front brake?

options.text: About 10 percent.
About 25 percent.
About 50 percent.
About 70 percent.

questions.explanation: The front brake is stronger than the rear brake. It supplies at least three-quarters of a motorcycle's total stopping power.

questions.question: Where should you ride in your lane when being passed?

options.text: In the center of the lane.
In the left portion of the lane.
In the right portion of the lane.
Weave among all three portions of the lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: In the center of the lane.
questions.explanation: Ride in the center of your lane when being passed. Riding on the side closest to the passing vehicle increases crash risk. Riding on the far side may make the other driver merge back too early.

questions.question: A rectangular sign can be a:

options.text: School crossing sign.
Railroad crossing sign.
Stop sign.
Speed limit sign.

questions.explanation: Speed limit signs are rectangular with white background and black letters. These signs tell drivers what rules to follow. You must obey the rules on these signs.

questions.question: When riding in a group and passing another vehicle, you should:

options.text: Let one rider fully pass before the next rider starts to pass.
Let several riders pass the other vehicle at the same time.
Have the last rider wave to signal no more motorcycles are coming.
Pass in a staggered formation.

questions.correctAnswerText: Let one rider fully pass before the next rider starts to pass.
questions.explanation: In a group, riders should pass one at a time. Each rider must finish passing and return to the group formation before the next rider begins to pass.

questions.question: A shatter-resistant face shield:

options.text: Can protect your face during a crash.
Only protects you from dirt.
Does not protect as much as goggles.
Should not be used with a helmet.

questions.correctAnswerText: Can protect your face during a crash.
questions.explanation: A plastic shatter-resistant face shield protects your entire face in a crash. Goggles only protect your eyes. A face shield also protects you from dirt, dust, insects, rain, and rocks.

questions.question: Your lane position should:

options.text: Keep other drivers from sharing your lane.
Give you a nice view of scenery.
Place you in other drivers' blind spots.
Hide your intentions from other drivers.

questions.correctAnswerText: Keep other drivers from sharing your lane.
questions.explanation: A good lane position keeps you safe. It keeps you out of blind spots, helps other drivers see you, helps you avoid road hazards, protects you from wind blasts, and gives you an escape route. Position yourself to discourage other drivers from entering your lane.

questions.question: When using a sidecar to carry a load, you should:

options.text: Let the load move freely.
Secure the load so it does not shift.
Place the load loose in the seat.
Secure the load at the front of the sidecar.

questions.correctAnswerText: Secure the load so it does not shift.
questions.explanation: Secure your load so it cannot move and affect how your motorcycle handles. Place the load toward the back of the sidecar to prevent the nose from tipping up during sharp left turns.

questions.question: A helmet will not protect you best if:

options.text: It is certified by the DOT.
It fits snugly.
It is free of damage.
It has cracks.

questions.explanation: Your helmet must have a DOT certification and fit snugly all the way around. It must have no damage such as cracks, loose padding, or damaged straps.

questions.question: Riding next to another vehicle:

options.text: Can put you in the driver's blind spot.
Is safer than riding behind the vehicle.
Is safe because your escape routes are limited.
Should only be done during the day.

questions.correctAnswerText: Can put you in the driver's blind spot.
questions.explanation: Do not ride beside another vehicle because you may be in the driver's blind spot. The driver cannot see you and may turn into your lane. Also, the vehicle blocks your escape route if a hazard appears.

questions.question: When passing another vehicle:

options.text: You can complete the pass in a no passing zone.
You can go up to 10 mph over the speed limit.
You must start and finish the pass in a passing zone.
You must complete the pass on the shoulder.

questions.correctAnswerText: You must start and finish the pass in a passing zone.
questions.explanation: Always pass within the speed limit and only in areas where passing is safe and legal.

questions.question: The best way to stop quickly is to:

options.text: Use the front brake only.
Use the front brake first.
Release the throttle and use the front brake.
Use both brakes together.

questions.explanation: To stop quickly, apply the front and rear brakes at the same time.

questions.question: When a rider extends their left arm straight out to the left, it means:

options.text: The rider plans to turn left.
The rider is about to stop.
The rider plans to turn right.
The rider is about to slow down.

questions.correctAnswerText: The rider plans to turn left.
questions.explanation: Riders can use hand signals instead of turn signals. When a rider's left arm is extended straight out to the left, it signals a left turn or a change to the left lane.

questions.question: Most motorcycles have:

options.text: Only a front brake.
Only a rear brake.
Brakes in both the front and rear.
Three brakes: one in front, one in rear, and an emergency brake.

questions.correctAnswerText: Brakes in both the front and rear.
questions.explanation: Motorcycles have two brakes. One brake controls the front wheel and one controls the rear wheel.

questions.question: Braking while turning is:

options.text: Easier than braking on a straight road.
Harder than braking on a straight road.
Done safely by using only the front brake.
Done safely by using only the rear brake.

questions.correctAnswerText: Harder than braking on a straight road.
questions.explanation: Braking while turning is harder than braking on a straight road. You can use both brakes while turning, but you must know the correct technique and be very careful.

questions.question: When braking, you should:

options.text: Use only one brake in non-emergency situations.
Use both brakes only when riding on wet pavement.
Use both brakes every time.
Use only the front brake.

questions.explanation: Always use both brakes when you slow down or stop.

questions.question: Where is the rear brake pedal located?

options.text: On the left handlebar
On the right handlebar
Near the left footrest
Near the right footrest

questions.explanation: The rear brake pedal is located near the right footrest.

questions.question: More than half of all motorcycle crashes involve:

options.text: Riders with less than six months of experience on their motorcycle.
Faulty ignition systems.
Distractions caused by passengers.
Accidents that happen at night.

questions.correctAnswerText: Riders with less than six months of experience on their motorcycle.
questions.explanation: Be very careful when riding a motorcycle that is new to you. Most motorcycle crashes happen to riders with less than six months of experience on that specific bike.
